chunks: Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Shadawayh al-Mu'addib (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Ja'far al-Himyari narrated to us from his father, from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim, from Zakariyya ibn Muhammad al-Mu'min, from al-Mushma'ill al-Asadi. He said:

I went on Hajj one year, then I went to Abu Abdillah al-Sadiq, Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both). He said: Where have you come from, O Mushma'ill? I said: May I be your sacrifice! I was on Hajj. He said: Do you know what reward the pilgrim receives? I said: I do not know until you teach me.

He said: When a servant circumambulates this House seven times, prays its two rak'ahs, and performs the sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwa, God records six thousand good deeds for him, erases six thousand sins from him, raises him six thousand levels, fulfills six thousand of his worldly needs, and reserves the same for the Hereafter.

I said to him: May I be your sacrifice! This is truly a great amount! He said: Shall I not inform you of something greater than that? I said: Of course. So he (peace be upon him) said: Fulfilling the need of a believing person is better than a Hajj, another Hajj, another Hajj — until he counted ten Hajj pilgrimages.

key_terms.أُسْبُوعًا: seven circuits of tawaf around the Ka'bah; one full round of circumambulation is called a shawt, and seven make an usbuw
key_terms.الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةِ: al-Safa and al-Marwa: two hills in Mecca between which pilgrims perform sa'i (seven walks), commemorating Hajar's search for water
key_terms.حَاجَة امرئ مؤمن: fulfilling the need of a believing person; used as a technical concept emphasizing brotherhood and mutual aid among the faithful
key_terms.حَسَنَة: a single good deed or merit recorded by God; contrasted with sayyi'a (sin)

ai.seo_question: What is the reward for helping a believer compared to performing Hajj according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) presents a striking hierarchy of rewards: each complete set of Hajj rituals (tawaf, prayer, sa'i) earns 6,000 good deeds, forgiveness of 6,000 sins, 6,000 ranks of elevation, and 6,000 worldly and otherworldly needs fulfilled. Yet even this extraordinary reward is surpassed by fulfilling a believer's need — which the Imam repeatedly emphasizes is better than even ten Hajj pilgrimages. The hadith addresses al-Mushma'ill al-Asadi shortly after his return from Hajj, using the occasion to reframe the hierarchy of Islamic virtues: service to fellow believers is among the highest acts of worship.
